q: One word opens the names of a long list of Italian, Iberian and Greek wines, white and red, sweet and dry, and most of the vines behind them turn out not to be related to each other. Which word?
opts: Garganega
Malvasia
Verdicchio
Vermentino
exp: It is a group of varieties rather than a variety, and Malvasia Bianca, Malvasia di Candia, Malvasia Istriana and Malvasia di Lipari are separate vines with separate parentages, while Puglia's Malvasia Nera turns out to be a natural cross of Negroamaro with another Malvasia. The word appears to travel back to a Greek port that shipped sweet wine to Venice, and it attached itself to whatever was in the barrel. A label carrying it therefore promises far less than it looks as though it should.

q: One estate bottles a single vineyard twice, printing Syrah on one label and Shiraz on the other, and the vines, the clone and the soil are identical. What is that pair of words doing?
opts: Signalling the style the buyer should expect, since both name one variety
Separating an estate-grown wine from one made with bought-in fruit
Marking two different clones of the one variety
Separating an oaked bottling from an unoaked one
exp: Usage rather than law has attached an expectation to each word, the French form suggesting pepper, freshness and restraint and the Australian form suggesting riper, sweeter, fuller fruit. Nothing binds a producer to either reading, so the choice is a convention the label trusts the buyer to understand. Growers working cool sites outside France very often choose the French form for precisely that reason.

q: A list is to carry one variety twice, from two countries, without printing the same grape name in both places. Which pairing does that?
opts: A Sicilian Nero d'Avola and a Puglian Negroamaro
A Rioja Tempranillo and a Tuscan Sangiovese
A Puglian Primitivo and a Californian Zinfandel
A Beaujolais Gamay and a Loire Gamay
exp: The two names belong to one variety, registered separately in each country long before anybody compared the plants, so a list can show it twice without repeating a word. Gamay is Gamay in both of the places named, and the remaining pairs are genuinely different vines. It makes a useful flight, since a guest meets one grape in two climates and tastes what the place did to it.

q: Handed a Spanish red labelled Garnacha and a southern French red labelled Grenache, a guest asks whether the two are related. What is the correct answer?
opts: No, two closely related varieties descended from a common Pyrenean parent
No, the French vine is a crossing bred from the Spanish one
Yes, the same variety under Spanish and French spellings
Yes, but only where the French wine states its grape on the label
exp: The vine is Spanish in origin, crossed the Pyrenees centuries ago and picked up a French spelling on the way. It is among the most widely planted black grapes anywhere and turns out everything from pale dry pink to sweet fortified red, so a shared identity guarantees nothing at all about style. Its modern reputation rests on old low-yielding bush vines rather than on the volume it was long grown for.

q: The corner of a Cahors label carries the word Cot, and the guest holding the bottle recognises nothing on it. Which grape does that word name?
opts: Tannat
Malbec
Merlot
Fer Servadou
exp: Cot is the older French name and Cahors has used it since long before the wider world learned the other one, so both turn up on labels there. Touraine growers in the Loire use it as well. The wine most drinkers associate with the better-known name is made a hemisphere away, which is why one word travelled and the other stayed at home.

q: Labels from one Alpine Italian province print two names for the same pale red grape, one Italian and one German, often on a single bottle. What explains the doubling?
opts: One name is used for the still wine and the other for the sparkling
The province is officially bilingual, so grapes are named twice
The two names mark two different clones grown there
One name belongs to the co-operatives and the other to private estates
exp: Alto Adige and Sudtirol are one place in the two official languages, and villages, denominations and varieties all carry an Italian name and a German one. The grape in question makes a pale, light, low-tannin red drunk young and mostly drunk locally. Reading such a label means recognising a translation rather than hunting for a second wine.

q: A Priorat back label prints Samso, a Rioja one prints Mazuelo and a Languedoc one prints Carignan. What links the three words?
opts: All three name a style of red wine rather than any single grape
All three name varieties bred from one common parent
All three are permitted blending partners within one appellation
All three name a single black variety, in three languages
exp: The vine is high in acid, high in tannin and enormously productive, which is why it was planted by the hectare for bulk wine and then pulled out again. Where old bush vines survive and crop very little it is taken seriously once more. A Spanish denomination shares one of the names, both of them taken from the same Aragonese town, and is planted more to other varieties than to that grape, which catches people out.

q: Growers in Chinon call the grape Breton, and growers on Bordeaux's Right Bank call the same vine Bouchet. Which variety are both of them talking about?
opts: Cabernet Franc
Merlot
Malbec
Cabernet Sauvignon
exp: Breton has nothing to do with Brittany and is thought to record the name of the man said to have spread the vine through the Loire, while Bouchet is the old Libournais word and survives inside several estate names there. One variety, two districts, and wines that resemble each other very little. It is a clean reminder that a synonym tells you about naming and never about style.

q: Two neutral, high-acid whites reach the same buyer, one labelled Ugni Blanc in France and one labelled Trebbiano Toscano in Italy. What is the relationship between them?
opts: Two different varieties belonging to one family of Mediterranean whites
A single vine, called Ugni Blanc in France and Trebbiano Toscano in Italy
One variety, though only the Italian name may lawfully be printed in Europe
A French crossing bred from the Italian variety and Colombard
exp: It is among the most widely planted white grapes in the world and gives a wine so neutral that it is usually blended away or used as a base rather than bottled under its own name. Italy attaches a regional word to it, so Trebbiano Toscano, Trebbiano Romagnolo and Trebbiano d'Abruzzo look like one family and are in fact several distinct vines. That makes the Italian name considerably less precise than the French one.

q: Sent back for looking faintly coppery rather than water-white, a glass of Pinot Grigio comes to you at the pass. What is the correct explanation?
opts: Oxidation in the bottle has browned a white that should be pale
The skins hold a pink-grey pigment, and the juice was left on them
A little red wine was blended in, which is how a copper tint is made
The wine spent a long time in new oak, which stained it a faint copper
exp: Pressing quickly gives the pale wine most drinkers expect and leaving the juice on the skins gives a coppery one, so the colour is a decision rather than an accident. Italian producers call the deliberate version ramato, meaning coppered, and it is a long-standing style in the north-east. The same variety under its French name is more often made in a fuller, weightier manner again.

q: A Ligurian white labelled Pigato, a Piedmontese one labelled Favorita and a Provencal one labelled Rolle all prove to share one identity. Which better-known name covers the three of them?
opts: Cortese
Arneis
Vermentino
Verdicchio
exp: Local selections differ a little in the vineyard, which is why each district defends its own word, but the vine behind them is single. It grows right around the north-western Mediterranean and on the islands, and the widely known name is what most export labels now carry. Provence in particular keeps its own word on the bottle, while Sardinia and Tuscany print the international one, so which name a buyer meets depends on where the wine was made.

q: An Italian list offers Riesling Renano and Riesling Italico, and a guest asks for the true Rhine grape. Which of the two should be poured?
opts: Neither, since both name crossings bred from Riesling
Either, since the two phrases mean the same thing
Riesling Renano
Riesling Italico
exp: Renano means of the Rhine and marks the genuine article. The other name belongs to an unrelated high-acid white that carries a different name in nearly every country between Austria and the Black Sea, and nothing but that second word separates the two on an Italian label. Borrowing a famous variety's name for an unrelated grape was ordinary practice, and although modern rules stop new ones being coined the old names stand, which is why Riesling Italico is still a name an Italian label may carry.

q: A northern Italian label prints Pinot Bianco and a German one prints Weissburgunder, and a guest assumes two different grapes. Which single variety is in both bottles?
opts: Pinot Blanc
Chardonnay
Pinot Gris
Chenin Blanc
exp: Both names translate the French one word for word, the Italian directly and the German by way of the family name it uses for the whole Pinot group. The wine is a quiet, appley, medium-bodied white that suffers from being compared with Chardonnay, which it faintly resembles and is regularly mistaken for. Recognising the translation is most of what reading such a label requires.

q: A Sicilian white labelled Grecanico and a Veneto white from the hills around Soave turn out to be one vine. Which name does the Veneto print?
opts: Verdicchio
Garganega
Grillo
Trebbiano
exp: The match was established only recently, ending a long assumption that a Sicilian grape whose name suggests Greece could have nothing to do with a Venetian one. The vine ripens late, keeps its acidity and gives a wine of almonds and white flowers in both places, though the climates could hardly be less alike. Names that gesture at an origin are among the least reliable evidence in the whole subject.

q: Three whites reach one table from Spain, the Portuguese Atlantic islands and the Marche, and their grape names differ by only a handful of letters. What is the relationship between the three vines?
opts: All three are crossings from a single parent
All three are colour mutations of one variety
All three are regional names for one variety
There is none; the resemblance is in the names alone
exp: Verdejo, Verdelho and Verdicchio all take their names from the green tinge of a ripening berry, and words built on that root have attached themselves to unrelated vines right around the Mediterranean. A shared word root looks like evidence and is not. Cases of this kind stood open for centuries, since a name carries no record of where the cuttings actually came from.

q: A story often told at the table has one famous black grape carried to France from a Persian city whose name it echoes. Where did the vine actually come from?
opts: It is a natural crossing of two obscure French varieties
It reached France from Persia, carried by returning crusaders
It is a colour mutation of Grenache
It was bred deliberately in a nineteenth-century French nursery
exp: The parents are Dureza from the Ardeche and Mondeuse Blanche from Savoie, both local, both obscure, which puts the grape's origin squarely in France. Romantic origin stories cling to grape names because a name that sounds like a distant place invites one. The lesson generalises: a name is evidence of what people once believed and not of where a vine came from.
